needsYou.title: Say the word and I switch the creative register on for your account and roll your cyborg brief through it
needsYou.productImpact: The register you asked for after the court ("C with the framing fixed") is built and switched off for everyone. Turned on for your account only, a creative brief — your cyborg — compiles as YOUR WORDS FIRST, then the same framing, camera and realism rules that gave sheet B its detail, then one line of variation per candidate on the open things only (never on anything you stated). Ordinary briefs — a dad, a runway model, a surgeon — are untouched even with it on: the product's own reader has to find a real creature/hardware/world element in your words, in your words, or it takes today's road. Nothing changes for any other account.
needsYou.workedExample: Today your 553-character cyborg brief becomes a 13,600-character prompt in which your words are 3.4% of the text, and the sheet came back timid and bearded. Under the register the same 160-credit roll sends your brief verbatim at the top, then the house framing block (mid-torso, 2:3, hair inside the frame — the lock arm C lost), the camera and skin-realism rules, and then per candidate a line like: THIS CANDIDATE: older wear — the ports and seams scuffed and oxidised at their edges. Eight candidates, same price, and the strip lands in your gallery next to the court's so you can judge conviction and spread side by side.

options.label: Hold
options.consequence: It stays dark. Nothing changes for anyone; the build is merged (PR #94) and switched off, waiting for your word.

needsYou.recommendation: Flip it. The roll is the only way to find out what you asked to find out — how close the register gets to your raw prompt with the framing held — and off is byte-identical to today, so there is nothing to undo if you dislike the strip.

needsYou.title: GitHub's own leak-blocker is ON for the Drape repository — done on your "Turn it on"
needsYou.productImpact: Tonight's check catches a leaked key when a change is proposed. GitHub can also refuse the upload itself, seconds earlier, before the key is anywhere anyone else can see it. That switch is off on the repository — the block we hit tonight came from a setting on the uploading account, which a different account would not have.
needsYou.workedExample: When I deliberately uploaded a fake OpenRouter key to test the new check, GitHub refused the upload outright ("push declined … OpenRouter API Key"). That refusal was luck of the account, not a property of the repo: GitHub → Drape repository → Settings → Code security → "Push protection" is OFF. Turning it on makes that refusal apply to every account and every branch.
needsYou.recommendation: Turn it on. Repository settings are yours, not the team's; it is free and has no effect on customers.

eyeItems.title: The creative-register court — eight arms of your cyborg brief (C′ rerun valid as of 26 Aug 02:35)
eyeItems.question: Does the creative register (arm C) reach your raw prompt’s conviction (arm A, and your two reference frames) while keeping sheet structure? Check each frame against your own list: jaw plate present and prominent, amber eye glowing, porcelain committed, no beards you never asked for, build spread not converged, wardrobe line obeyed. Refusal counts are under each strip’s caption.

frames.caption: Your reference frame 1 — the conviction bar, made by your own raw prompt.
Your reference frame 2 — the second raw-prompt frame.
Your raw prompt + your seven words of frame, re-made tonight. 0 of 3 refused. This is the bar the candidate must reach.
Today’s full compile, through the real entrance. 0 of 3 refused — but look: beards you never asked for on all three, t-shirts against the bare-chested ask, and the hardware gone timid.

THE CANDIDATE — the creative register: your words verbatim, a minimal frame, a per-slice variance card. 1 of 3 refused. Hardware committed — but the mid-torso framing line was ignored (full body delivered), so the lean frame loses locks the old scaffolding held.
The candidate minus the variance card. 2 OF 3 REFUSED — the card appears to protect against refusals as well as buying spread.
The candidate plus the one-sentence category block. 2 of 3 refused.

RERUN, now valid: the same three compiles as B with every house block cut to its first clause and YOUR facts kept word for word (12,500 → 3,300 characters). 0 of 3 refused. Against B: the beards, the shirts and the missing porcelain are still here — shortening did not fix them, so those answers are WRONG, not long. What it bought is conviction: a solid jaw plate in frames 1 and 3, and a tighter mid-torso frame.
The writer’s room: “cyber-goth girl with an eyepatch”, authored into rich concepts, rendered. 1 of 3 refused; the author gave 4 concepts of the 8 asked.
The same thin brief through today’s compile — the control for the writer’s room.

pipeline.title: Warden — patrol #1: the security scanner now checks every change before it can merge; the dead-code reader runs nightly (#97)
pipeline.note: Team tooling only — nothing a customer sees. Every pull request now has to pass a security-shape scanner (semgrep) before it can merge, and it was proven able to fail: a deliberately planted dangerous line turned the check red, and the same tree without it went green. Its honest limit is written down: it does NOT catch a shell command built from a web request, so the reviewer stays the control for that class. The dead-code reader now runs on its own every night at 1am and leaves a reading for the Janitor. First security baseline recorded: no leaked secrets across all 2,668 commits, no scanner findings, all access-control tests green (26/26). This patrol took three attempts — two shift processes died just before writing their close — which is exactly the class the Retro's #101 guard is for.

pipeline.title: Janitor — patrol #1: the machine's leftovers cleared, the dead-code reading turned into four cards (#96)
pipeline.note: Housekeeping only — nothing a customer sees. Four abandoned workspace folders from earlier shifts deleted from the machine; four leftover login tokens minted by test drives (never committed) deleted, and the two scratch folders they lived in are now ignored by git so they can never be committed by accident (PR #104). The code-scanner's first reading became four cards for later: 40 unused UI components carrying 21 unused packages (#105), 11 other unused files confirmed by three separate readers (#106), 7 unused dev packages — two of them a typo from day one (#107), and 173 unused functions to be sorted into never-used vs. quietly disconnected before anything is deleted (#108). The old output folder cleanup (#8) got 4 more folders gone before the disk hung again; 33 remain, harmless.

pipeline.title: Retro — patrol #1: the night's reports checked against what actually happened, and five repeat problems given a fix each (#95)
pipeline.note: Team process only — nothing a customer sees. Five shift reports were opened claim by claim: four were true to the commit, the receipt and the test run; one (the 07:00 shift) said it had merged the register, shipped your page and cleaned up, and had done none of it — its process died mid-close with a placeholder where the receipt goes. The fix is mechanical (#101): the runner stamps every close AFTER the shift ends, so a dead shift can no longer leave "done" standing. Four other repeats got a guard card each (#100 stale-map stalls, #102 two sessions committing into one tree, #103 a hidden byte that silently disables a security config, and the worktree cleanup quirk noted on #96). Also checked: every security tool added last night traces to a card filed hours before it — nobody was building out of boredom.

pipeline.title: A second automatic security reader now scans every proposed change for known-dangerous code shapes (#33)
pipeline.note: in this deploy; team tooling, nothing a customer sees. It looks for the classic mistakes — building database queries from text, running user text as code, writing user text straight into a page. I did not trust it until it had been caught out: I planted two dangerous lines and it found both; the same plant in a throw-away script folder was correctly ignored. It also MISSED one planted shape (running a shell command from a web request), which is written on its record page rather than hidden. Its first read of the product: four notes, all one harmless pattern in the homepage image route — and opening that file to annotate them found a small real bug: asking for a hero image called 'constructor' got a server error instead of a plain 'not found'. Fixed, with a test that fails on the old code.

pipeline.title: The team's dead-code detector is in — one command lists every file, export and dependency nothing uses (#34)

Proven both ways before it counted — a planted dead file and a planted dead export were both caught, and the five modules our older map once wrongly called unused (both login routes among them) are correctly left alone. First reading: 51 unused files (40 of them unused UI primitives from the component kit), 34 unused packages, 174 unused exports. Nothing was deleted; the Janitor's first patrol takes it from here.
